sermon:
There is a particular kind of silence that falls in a room after a funeral, when the casseroles are gone and the cards have been read and the person everyone leaned on is no longer there to lean on. Israel stood in that silence. Moses was dead. The man who had argued with Pharaoh, split the sea, carried the tablets down the mountain, and interceded for a people who deserved fire instead of forty more years was gone. And into that silence God speaks to a second-in-command named Joshua.

**The Promise Does Not Die With the Man**

Notice how God opens. "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel" (Joshua 1:2). God names the death plainly. He does not soften it. But the death of Moses is not the death of the promise. The land was never Moses's gift to give; it was God's, sworn to Abraham four centuries earlier. We tend to bind God's faithfulness to particular people, the pastor who baptized us, the parent who prayed for us, the friend who carried us. When they die, our faith feels orphaned. But the covenant was never resting on their shoulders. It was resting on God's. The promise outlives the man because the promise was never the man's to begin with.

**Courage Is Tethered to a Book and a Presence**

Three times God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous. We read that as a pep talk, a motivational poster for the anxious. It is nothing of the kind. The courage God commands is not self-generated nerve. It is fastened to two things. First, the Book. "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night" (Joshua 1:8). The courage to take a land of fortified cities and iron chariots comes not from military confidence but from a man muttering Scripture under his breath until it becomes the grammar of his thinking. Second, the presence. "Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you" (Joshua 1:5). Joshua is not brave because the enemy is weak. He is brave because he is not alone.

I have to confess that my own courage is usually counterfeit. It runs on the size of the obstacle and the strength of my preparation, and it collapses the moment I am outmatched. I am brave when I think I can win. That is not faith. That is arithmetic. God offered Joshua a courage that holds even when the math fails, because it is anchored outside the self.

**The Jordan Is Still in Front of You**

Here is the part we want to skip. God says arise and go, but the Jordan is at flood stage and the cities are real. Faith does not remove the river. It commands you to cross it. The presence of God is not a guarantee of ease. It is a guarantee of company. Joshua had to put his feet in the water before anything parted.

And this is where the name itself preaches. Joshua, in Hebrew, is Yehoshua, the same name that comes to us in Greek as Yeshua, as Jesus. The first Joshua led a people into a land of rest that was always temporary, always contested, always slipping back into idolatry. He could deliver geography. He could not deliver hearts. The second Joshua, the true and better one, leads His people into a rest that does not erode. The letter to the Hebrews says it outright: if the first Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day. Jesus is the leader who crosses the deeper Jordan ahead of us, who goes into death first, and who does not leave us or forsake us, not because we are strong, but because He is.

So when the person you leaned on is gone, and the river is high, and your courage is only arithmetic, hear the word given over a fresh grave at the edge of a flood. The God who buried Moses is going with you. The Book is in your mouth. The land is already given.

The promise outlives the man.

Two spies cross into enemy territory on a reconnaissance mission and end up in the one house in Jericho where nobody asks questions about strangers, the house of a prostitute named Rahab. We should not rush past how scandalous this is. The first ally Israel finds in the promised land is a Canaanite, a woman, and a woman whose trade the law condemns. Grace did not knock at the temple. It knocked at the brothel.

**The Confession Israel Keeps Forgetting**

The king of Jericho hears the spies are in the city and sends to Rahab to give them up. She hides them under flax on her roof and lies to the king's men, and then she says something that should stop us cold. "The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11). A Canaanite prostitute, raised in a city of many gods, confesses the monotheism that Israel itself could barely hold onto. Read forward a few chapters and Israel will be stealing devoted things and worshiping the gods of the land. Read back and they were melting gold into a calf at the foot of the mountain. Here, in a pagan city under judgment, a woman states the creed plainly. She had heard what God did at the Red Sea forty years before, and unlike the kings of Canaan who heard the same reports and only trembled, she believed.

This indicts me. I have sat in church my whole adult life and I forget, by Tuesday, what Rahab grasped on the strength of a rumor. She had less light than I have and more faith. The people with every advantage often hold the truth most loosely. The people with no standing at all sometimes seize it with both hands because they have nothing else to hold.

**The Scarlet Cord in the Window**

Rahab asks for mercy, not just for herself but for her father and mother, her brothers and sisters, all who belong to them. The spies agree on one condition. "Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window" (Joshua 2:18). A red cord, hung where it could be seen, marking a house that judgment would pass over. We have seen this before. Blood on the doorposts in Egypt, the angel of death passing by. The scarlet in the window says the same thing the blood on the lintel said: those inside this mark are covered, not because they earned it, but because a sign of redemption is hanging where God can see it.

Notice also that her faith gathers a household. She does not run alone. She drags her whole family inside the line the cord draws. Saving faith is rarely a private transaction. It reaches for the people you love and pulls them toward the covering.

**Grace Reaches the Wrong House First**

We like to imagine grace flowing from the religious center outward to the margins, from the deserving to the desperate. Joshua tells the opposite story. Grace ran past the respectable households of Israel's own genealogy and arrived first at the wrong address, in the wrong city, in the wrong woman. And then God did something with that wrong house that He never did with the right ones.

Turn to the first chapter of Matthew and read the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and there she is. Rahab. The Canaanite. The prostitute. The mother of Boaz, who married Ruth, another outsider, in the line that runs down to David and finally to Christ. God did not merely spare Rahab. He wrote her into the bloodline of the Savior. The woman behind the scarlet cord became a grandmother of the One whose own blood would hang, in a sense, in every window of the world.

If you have ever believed you are the wrong house, too far gone, too compromised, too late, hear this. Grace has a habit of knocking at the wrong house first, and of moving in to stay.

Grace reaches the wrong house first.

Picture a river at flood stage. Not a placid stream you could wade, but the Jordan in spring, when the snowmelt off Hermon swells it past its banks and the current would take a grown man off his feet. Now picture an entire nation, women and children and livestock and the old, told to walk across it. There is no bridge. There is no boat. There is only a command and a box of acacia wood covered in gold.

**The Ark Goes In First**

God's instruction is precise. The priests carrying the ark of the covenant are to go ahead of the people, and the moment their feet touch the water's edge, the river will stop. "And as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water... the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap" (Joshua 3:15-16). The order matters. The water did not part and then the priests stepped onto dry ground. The priests stepped into the flood while it was still a flood, and only then did it stand up in a heap.

The ark went in first. The ark was where God's presence met His people, the seat of mercy, the place of the covenant. And God sent His own presence into the danger ahead of the nation. He did not wave them across from the far bank. He went into the water first and held it back so they could follow on dry ground.

This is the rhythm of faith that I resist with everything in me. I want the river dry before I commit my feet. I want the evidence before the obedience, the parted water before the wet sandal. God's people learned otherwise. The priests stood in the riverbed holding the ark, the symbol of God's presence, while the whole nation passed, and the water did not move until it had something heavy resting in it.

**Stones for Children Not Yet Born**

When the crossing is done, God gives a strange command. Twelve men, one from each tribe, are to take twelve stones from the middle of the riverbed where the priests stood, and pile them on the far bank. Why? "When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them" (Joshua 4:6-7). The miracle was not for the generation that crossed. It was for the generation that had not yet been born.

We are so consumed by our own experience of God that we forget we are building a memory for people who will never have seen what we have seen. The stones were a sermon in rock, set there so that a child decades later would ask the question and a parent would have to tell the story again. Faith is not only lived. It is handed down. And we are negligent stewards of it. We have the experiences and we pile no stones. We cross our Jordans and leave nothing on the bank, and our children grow up knowing we believe something but never knowing why.

**The Lord of All the Earth**

Joshua told them, before the crossing, why this would happen: "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan" (Joshua 3:11). The Lord of all the earth. Not a tribal deity of a wandering people, but the One who owns the river and the land on both sides of it.

And here is the deeper crossing the stones point toward. There is another Jordan, the cold river of death, and another One who went into it first. Jesus stepped into the waters of judgment ahead of His people, not symbolically but bodily, and held them back by standing in them. He went down into the grave and stood there until the whole company of the redeemed could pass over onto resurrection ground. The ark went in first. The true ark, the One in whom the presence of God dwelt fully, went in first.

So pile your stones. Tell the children. And when you reach a river you cannot cross, look for the ark already standing in the middle of it.

The ark goes in first.

There is an old and persistent error in the human heart that says preparation for God means getting busy. Sharpen the sword, draft the plan, take the hill. Israel stood on the near edge of Jericho, the most fortified city in the region, with the memory of forty wasted years behind them, and the first thing God commanded was not a strategy session. It was surgery. And then a meal.

**Circumcised Before the Conquest**

God tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise the people, because the entire generation born in the wilderness had never received the covenant sign. "For all the people who came out had been circumcised, but all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness... had not been circumcised" (Joshua 5:5). Think about the timing. The enemy is in front of them. The smart move, by any military logic, is to keep every fighting man whole and ready. Instead God renders the entire army temporarily incapable of fighting, sore and recovering, within sight of a hostile city.

This is offensive to the way I operate. I would have circumcised them after the victory, as a thanksgiving. God did it before, as a precondition. The point is unmistakable: God will not let His people take the land until they wear the mark of belonging to Him. Consecration is not the reward for conquest. It is the requirement before it. Before you do anything for God, you must first belong to God, and that belonging is cut into you, not chosen as a convenience.

**The Reproach of Egypt Rolled Away**

Then God says something that gives the place its name. "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you. And so the name of that place is called Gilgal" (Joshua 5:9). The reproach of Egypt. The shame of slavery, the identity of a people who had been someone's property, the lingering smell of the brick pits. For forty years they had wandered as a generation that had never been marked, never fully claimed, still carrying the old shame. And God rolls it away, not gradually, not after they prove themselves, but at Gilgal, before the first battle.

We carry our reproach of Egypt longer than we need to. The old life, the old shame, the identity God has already removed but we keep dragging behind us like a name we refuse to stop answering to. God rolled it away. The question is why I keep picking it back up.

**The Manna Stops and the Land Feeds Them**

The next detail is quiet and enormous. They keep the Passover, and the day after, they eat the produce of the land, unleavened bread and roasted grain. "And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel" (Joshua 5:12). For forty years bread had fallen from the sky every morning. Now it stops, because the land itself feeds them. The provision changes form. The wilderness diet of miracle ends, and the settled diet of inheritance begins.

God's provision is not always dramatic. Sometimes He moves you from manna to harvest, from the miraculous to the ordinary, and the ordinary is no less His gift. We sometimes grieve when the manna stops, mistaking the change for abandonment. But the manna stopped because the promise had landed. They were home.

All of this prepares the heart to see Christ. We come to His table the same way Israel came to the land, not as conquerors who earned a seat but as people who must first be marked, must first have the reproach rolled away, must first be fed before we are sent. The true circumcision, Paul says, is of the heart, made without hands, accomplished in the cross of Christ. He is the One who rolls away our reproach and then sets us at His table. We do not fight our way to belonging. We are made to belong, and then we are sent.

Consecration comes before conquest.

A man stands near Jericho with a drawn sword. Joshua, a soldier to his bones, walks up and asks the only question a commander asks of an armed stranger on the eve of battle. "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" It is the question we always ask. Whose side are you on. And the answer he gets undoes everything.

**The Commander Takes No Side But His Own**

"No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come" (Joshua 5:14). No. Not on your side, not on theirs. The figure refuses the question entirely. He has not come to join Joshua's cause. He has come to take command of it. And Joshua, the general, falls on his face and is told to remove his sandals, because the ground is holy, the same words spoken to Moses at the bush.

We spend our lives trying to recruit God to our side. We pray as if the goal were to get heaven's endorsement on the campaign we have already chosen. The answer at Jericho strips that illusion bare. God does not take sides. God takes over. The question is never whether God is for us in the sense of backing our plans. The question is whether we will fall on our faces and let Him command. Joshua had to stop being the strategist and become the worshiper before he could win.

**Taken by Marching, Trumpets, and a Shout**

Then comes the strangest battle plan in military history. March around the city once a day for six days, priests blowing trumpets, the ark in the procession, and say nothing. On the seventh day, march around seven times, and then shout. That is the whole strategy. No siege engines, no scaling ladders, no breach in the wall by force. "So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown... the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city" (Joshua 6:20).

Why this absurd plan? Because God was making sure no one could claim the victory. There was no clever maneuver to credit, no commander's genius to celebrate. A week of walking and a shout. If Jericho falls to marching feet and trumpet blasts, then everyone knows who took the city. It was removed from the realm of human achievement on purpose.

I confess I find this method humiliating, and that is the point. I want to win in a way that lets me take a bow. God designs victories that leave me with nothing to bow about. The marching was obedience without advantage, faith with no visible mechanism, and that is exactly the kind of faith God honors, because it has nowhere to look but up.

**Devoted Whole to God**

The city was placed under the ban, devoted entirely to the LORD, its spoils not for Israel's enrichment but given over wholly to God, the first fruits of the land. The victory was His, so the plunder was His. Israel was not permitted to profit from what God had done. The only ones spared were Rahab and her household, the scarlet cord made good.

And here the commander with the drawn sword points us forward. There is another Captain of the Lord's host who came not to take our side but to take command, who won a victory by a method that looked like defeat, who triumphed not by force of arms but by surrender, by a death that emptied every human boast. The cross is the trumpet and the shout. The walls that fell were not Jericho's but the wall of hostility itself, broken down by a Savior who let Himself be devoted, given over wholly to God in our place.

So stop asking God to join your side. Take off your sandals. March when He says march, be silent when He says be silent, and shout when He says shout. And when the wall falls flat, remember you did not push it.

The victory was never ours.

After Jericho, Israel is unstoppable. Or so they think. They send a small force against a small town called Ai, confident, almost casual, and the men of Ai rout them and chase them down the slope and kill thirty-six. Joshua tears his clothes and falls on his face and asks God why. And God tells him to get up, because this is not a moment for prayer. There is sin in the camp.

**One Man's Theft, All Israel's Guilt**

The verdict from heaven is stunning in its scope. "Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them. They have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied" (Joshua 7:11). Israel has sinned. Not a man. Israel. One man, Achan, had taken from the devoted spoil of Jericho, a beautiful cloak, silver, a bar of gold, and buried it under his tent. He told no one. He thought it was private. And God held the entire nation guilty for the hidden act of one.

We do not believe this anymore. We are thoroughly modern people who believe that what I do in private is mine alone, that my secret sin harms no one but me. Achan believed that too, right up until thirty-six men lay dead because of what was buried under his tent floor. There is no such thing as private sin in the body of God's people. The hidden thing in one tent defeated the whole army at the gate of a town that should have fallen in an hour.

I want to insist that my concealed compromises are nobody's business. The story will not let me. The cloak under Achan's tent and the bodies on the slope of Ai are connected by a line I cannot cut. My hidden sin is never only mine. It weakens the camp I belong to, even when no one knows it is there.

**Named and Judged Before the Victory**

God's remedy is exposure. Tribe by tribe, clan by clan, family by family, the lot narrows until it falls on Achan, and he confesses. "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did" (Joshua 7:20). Then he names it precisely: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. The whole anatomy of sin in four verbs. He saw the beautiful cloak. He coveted it. He took it. He hid it. That is every sin I have ever committed, in order.

The judgment that follows is severe, and we recoil from it. But the point the text presses is this: God would not give Ai into Israel's hand until the sin was named and dealt with. Not managed, not minimized, not quietly forgiven in the dark. Named. There is no victory at Ai on the far side of a covered sin. The blessing waited for the confession.

**Only Then Was Ai Given**

And once the sin was judged, God spoke again to Joshua: "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you... See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai" (Joshua 8:1). The same town that routed them now falls. The difference was not strategy. The difference was that the camp had been cleansed.

Here is where the gospel both deepens and reverses the story. Achan teaches us that one man's sin made the whole people guilty, and we know that pattern from the beginning, from Adam, whose one trespass condemned us all. But the gospel announces a glorious reversal. If one man's hidden theft could defeat a nation, then one Man's open obedience could save one. Where Achan saw, coveted, took, and hid, Christ resisted, refused, gave, and was lifted up in plain sight for all to see. The devoted thing Achan stole, Christ became, devoted wholly to God, given over in our place, so that the camp could finally be clean.

Do not bury anything under your tent. It does not stay there.

Hidden sin defeats the whole camp.

The conquest of Canaan was not a weekend. We compress it in our minds into a montage of falling walls and shouting armies, but the book of Joshua is in fact a long, grinding account of campaigns north and south, of cities taken and retaken, of years of obedience that never resolved into a clean ending. Between the high drama of Jericho and the quiet of the inheritance lies a long stretch of ordinary faithfulness, and three things in it deserve our attention.

**The Law Read Aloud on Two Mountains**

After the early victories, Joshua does something that looks like a detour. He stops the campaign and gathers all Israel between two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, and reads the law aloud, the blessings and the curses, exactly as Moses commanded. "There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, with the women and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them" (Joshua 8:35). Every word. The women, the children, the foreigners. In the middle of a war, Joshua pauses to remind the nation that the land is held by covenant, not by conquest. They are not in Canaan because they are strong. They are in Canaan because they belong to a God who gave them words to live by, and the words come before the next battle.

We are always tempted to think the work is the point and the word is the interruption. Joshua reverses it. The reading of the law is not a break from the mission. It is the foundation the mission stands on.

**A Covenant Kept With Deceivers**

Then comes the Gibeonites, who hear what happened to Jericho and Ai and decide to survive by trickery. They come in worn-out sandals and moldy bread, pretending to be travelers from a distant country, and beg for a treaty. Israel, the text says pointedly, "did not ask counsel from the LORD" (Joshua 9:14), and makes a covenant with them. Three days later the deception is discovered. The Gibeonites are neighbors, not foreigners. And here is the remarkable thing: Israel keeps the covenant anyway. The leaders had sworn by the LORD, and a vow made to deceivers in the name of God is still a vow made in the name of God.

I find this convicting in an age that treats commitments as provisional, binding only as long as they serve me. Israel was deceived into a promise and kept it, because their word, once given before God, was not theirs to retract. They did not ask God before they spoke. That was their failure. But having spoken, they would not make God a liar to escape an inconvenient bond.

**From South to North, the Lord Fought**

The campaigns roll on. Kings ally against Israel, in the south and then in the north, and city by city the land is subdued. But the narrator keeps inserting one phrase, almost monotonously, lest we miss it. The reason for every victory is not Israel's tactics. "And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel... There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel" (Joshua 10:14).

The LORD fought for Israel. That is the verdict over the entire long obedience. The reading of the law, the keeping of an unwise vow, the years of campaigning, all of it rests on the fact that the real warrior in the story was God Himself. Israel marched and Israel fought, but the outcome was never in Israel's hands.

And this is the shape of the Christian life still. We are called to a long obedience, the unglamorous faithfulness of keeping our word, sitting under Scripture, doing the next thing God commands long after the excitement of conversion has cooled. But the One who fights for us is Jesus, the better Joshua, who does not merely give us a land but secures us an inheritance no enemy can take. The long obedience is real, and ours, and yet it rests entirely on the fact that He fought, and won, the war we could not.

The LORD fought for Israel.

The middle of the book of Joshua turns from battle to bookkeeping, and most of us skip it. Chapters of borders and boundary stones, this tribe gets this valley, that clan gets these towns, lists of cities most of us cannot pronounce. We treat it as the dull part. But buried in the tedium of the allotment is one of the most important truths in the whole book, and we miss it because we are bored.

**The Land Is Divided by Lot, Not by Merit**

The inheritance is not awarded to the tribes that fought hardest or bled most. It is divided by lot. "These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan... Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses" (Joshua 14:1-2). The casting of the lot was the deliberate removal of human merit from the equation. No tribe could say it earned the better portion. The boundaries fell where they fell because God assigned them, not because anyone deserved them. A tribe's standing in the conquest did not buy it a single extra acre.

We cannot stand this, because we are accountants of merit to our core. We believe the best portion should go to the hardest worker, and we believe it about heaven too. We assume our inheritance with God is graded, that the faithful get the better real estate, that we are negotiating our eternal portion by our performance. The lot says no. The inheritance is gift, distributed by the hand of God, and our striving did not earn the boundary lines.

**The Land Still Unconquered Is Still Divided**

Here is the detail that should arrest us. Much of the land being divided had not actually been taken yet. There were Canaanite cities still standing, enemies still in the hills, territory on the map that was, in fact, still in enemy hands. And God divides it anyway. He assigns to the tribes land they have not yet possessed, drawing boundary lines through territory still occupied by the people they are meant to drive out.

Why divide what you do not yet hold? Because the inheritance does not rest on what Israel has already seized. It rests on what God has already sworn. The gift is secured by the promise, not by the progress. The deed was signed in God's word long before the last city fell. Israel did not own the land because Israel had conquered it. Israel was given the land, and conquering was simply taking hold of what was already theirs by gift.

This reorders everything about how I live. I treat my standing with God as a function of how much ground I have actually taken in my sanctification, how much sin I have actually conquered, how far I have actually come. And on the days the enemy still holds half the territory, I conclude the inheritance is in doubt. The allotment corrects me. The land was divided while it was still occupied. My inheritance is settled by God's sworn gift, not by my completed conquest. I am given the whole portion before I have taken an inch of it.

**The Gift Precedes the Taking**

This is the deep grammar of grace, and it runs straight to Christ. Paul writes that we have been given an inheritance, sealed with the Spirit as a guarantee, while we are still in the middle of a land not fully taken. The Spirit is the down payment on a possession we do not yet hold in full. Our inheritance is not the wage we are slowly earning. It is the gift already deeded to us in Christ, signed in His blood, sworn by the God who cannot lie, even while the enemy still holds ground in us.

So we fight, yes. We take the territory of obedience city by city, year by year. But we fight from the inheritance, not for it. The boundary lines have already fallen for us in pleasant places. The deed is signed. What remains is to take hold of what is already, by gift, our own.

The gift precedes the taking.

Most men, at eighty-five, are asking for less. A smaller house, a quieter life, an easier road, the valley instead of the hill. Caleb, at eighty-five, walks up to Joshua in the middle of the land distribution and asks for a mountain. Not just any mountain. The hill country where the giants live, the very country whose inhabitants had terrified ten spies into faithlessness forty-five years earlier. Give me that, he says. Give me the hard one.

**Forty-Five Years on a Promise**

Caleb's claim rests on something that happened almost half a century before. He and Joshua had been among the twelve spies sent into the land, and when ten came back trembling about giants and walled cities, Caleb and Joshua came back saying the land was good and God would give it to them. The nation believed the ten, and an entire generation died in the wilderness for it. But Moses had sworn that Caleb's portion would be the land his feet had walked. Now Caleb collects. "And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years... I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me" (Joshua 14:10-11).

Forty-five years. Caleb carried a promise for forty-five years through a wilderness full of funerals, watching everyone his own age die in the sand, and he did not let go of it. We struggle to hold a promise for forty-five days. We pray for something, and when the answer does not come by the end of the month, we conclude God has forgotten, or never said it. Caleb is a rebuke to the short patience of my faith. He waited nearly five decades, and he waited without bitterness, and he waited without going soft.

**He Wholly Followed the LORD**

The phrase the text keeps attaching to Caleb is the key to him. He "wholly followed the LORD" (Joshua 14:8, 14:14). Wholly. Not mostly, not when convenient, not with the reservations most of us tuck into our discipleship. The same word used for the devoted things at Jericho, the things given over completely to God, is used for the man. Caleb was wholly devoted, holding nothing back, and that wholeness is why, at eighty-five, he asks for the giants instead of the easy valley.

This exposes me. My following is partial. I follow the LORD in the areas where it costs little and quietly negotiate exemptions in the areas where it costs much. I want the inheritance of a Caleb on the discipleship of a part-time disciple. But the strength to ask for the mountain at eighty-five comes only to the one who followed wholly at forty. The boldness of his old age was paid for by the wholeness of his middle years.

**Give Me This Mountain**

"So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said" (Joshua 14:12). He names the giants. He names the fortified cities. He does not pretend the mountain is empty. He looks straight at the thing that frightened a whole generation and asks to be given it, because the God who promised it is worth the giants on it.

There is a faith that asks God for the smooth places and a faith that asks Him for the hard country, and the difference between them is whether you believe the One who fights for you. Caleb wanted the mountain because the mountain was where God had promised to be with him, and a promise from God is worth more than a comfortable retirement.

And this points us to the One who, at the end of His own road, did not ask for the valley. Jesus set His face toward the hardest country of all, toward the cross, toward the giants of sin and death in their fortified city, and asked, in effect, to be given that mountain, so that He might drive out the enemy and secure the inheritance for us. He wholly followed the Father, holding nothing back, all the way up the worst hill there is.

So when you are old, and tired, and tempted to ask only for the easy valley, remember a man of eighty-five with a mountain on his lips.

Give me this mountain.

There is a particular nightmare in the ancient world that we have mostly forgotten. A man swings an axe, the head flies off the handle, and a bystander is killed. No malice, no intent, just a horror that happened in an instant. In a culture of blood vengeance, where the dead man's nearest kin had the right and the duty to hunt down the one who killed him, that axeman was as good as dead, even though he had murdered no one. Into that terror God builds something into the map of the promised land.

**Mercy Planted Into the Geography**

God commands cities of refuge, six of them, spread across the land so that one was always within reach. "that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood" (Joshua 20:3). The man who killed accidentally could run to one of these cities, state his case at the gate, and be taken in and protected until a fair trial. Mercy was not left to chance or to the mood of the moment. It was built into the geography, surveyed and assigned, so that no one in Israel was ever more than a desperate run away from a place of safety.

Think about what this says about the God who designed the land. He did not only give Israel cities to live in and fields to farm. He planted refuge into the terrain itself, anticipating the worst accidents of human life and providing for them before they happened. The God of Joshua is not only a warrior. He is a refuge-builder, weaving protection for the desperate into the very layout of the country.

I confess I do not think of God this way often enough. I imagine Him concerned with the conquest, the big movements, the battles. I forget that the same God ordered cities for the man who would one day need to run, the trembling, guilt-haunted person fleeing something he did not even mean to do. God thought of him in advance, and built him a door.

**The Levites Scattered Among the Tribes**

Alongside the cities of refuge, God commands towns for the Levites, the priestly tribe. But notice how they are distributed. The Levites receive no single territory of their own. Instead they are scattered, given towns in the midst of every other tribe. The tribe whose work was the worship of God and the teaching of His law was deliberately spread thin across the whole nation, so that no Israelite lived far from someone whose business was the things of God.

The Levites had no inheritance of land because the LORD was their inheritance. And their scattering meant that holiness was not quarantined in one region but salted through all of them. Every tribe had teachers of the law in its midst. This is how God keeps a people from drifting, by distributing those who carry His word into every corner instead of concentrating them in one safe enclave.

**Not One Word Has Failed**

And then the narrator, surveying all of it, the cities, the refuge, the Levite towns, the whole inheritance, lays down the verdict that crowns the book. "Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass" (Joshua 21:45). Not one word. Every promise God had spoken across the generations, from Abraham to Moses, had landed. The map itself was the proof. The cities of mercy and the scattered Levites were the fingerprints of a God who keeps His word down to the smallest detail.

This is where the refuge points us home. There is a final city of refuge, a final place to run for the guilty, and His name is Jesus. The writer to the Hebrews says we have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us. We are not the innocent axeman who killed by accident. We are guilty, and we run anyway, and the door is open anyway, because the One who is our refuge took the blood-vengeance we deserved onto Himself. The avenger has been satisfied at the cross, and the city gate stands open.

Not one word has failed.

A nation almost goes to war over a building. The conquest is finished, the land is divided, and the tribes east of the Jordan, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, head home across the river to their inheritance. And on their way out, at the edge of the Jordan, they build an altar. A great, imposing altar. And when the western tribes hear of it, they assemble the entire army to march against their own brothers.

**An Altar That Looks Like Rebellion**

The reaction is immediate and violent. To build an altar outside the one place God had appointed for sacrifice looked like apostasy, like setting up a rival worship, like the first crack of the nation splitting in two. The western tribes remember Achan, they remember the plague at Peor, they remember that the sin of a few can bring wrath on all. So they prepare for civil war over what looks like a betrayal of the covenant. "And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them" (Joshua 22:12).

We should sit with how close this came to bloodshed. Brothers who had fought side by side through the entire conquest are about to slaughter each other over a structure on a riverbank. And the whole crisis rests on an interpretation. They saw the altar and assumed they understood what it meant. They were wrong.

**They Send Before They Strike**

Here is the wisdom we so often lack. Before the army marches, they send a delegation, Phinehas and ten leaders, to ask. They go and they confront and they accuse, but they ask first. And the eastern tribes explain. They built no altar for sacrifice. They built it out of fear, fear that one day the western tribes would look across the river and say to their children, "What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? ...you have no portion in the LORD" (Joshua 22:24-25). The Jordan was a wide river, and they were afraid it would one day become a border in the heart, that their descendants would be cut off, told they did not belong. So they built a replica altar, not to sacrifice on, but to stand as a witness.

"It is a witness between us and you... It shall be a witness between us" (Joshua 22:27-28). Not an altar of rebellion. An altar of belonging. A monument that said: we, too, are part of this people, we, too, worship the LORD, do not let the river divide us.

How many wars in the church have been fought over an altar that was really a witness? How often have I assembled my army, marshaled my outrage, and prepared to strike a brother over something I never bothered to ask about? The eastern tribes built a witness against division, and the western tribes nearly turned it into the very division it was built to prevent, all because the instinct was to attack before inquiring. The thing that saved the nation from civil war was a question asked before a sword was drawn.

**Build Witnesses, Not Divisions**

The leaders hear the explanation, and the text says they were glad. The crisis dissolves. They name the altar, by some readings, Witness, "for it is a witness between us that the LORD is God." The thing built in fear of exclusion became a standing testimony of unity.

This is the calling of God's people still. We are forever tempted to build divisions, to read the worst into one another's worship, to mistake a brother's different practice for betrayal and march out the army. The gospel calls us to the harder, slower work of building witnesses, monuments to the truth that we belong to the same Lord across whatever river runs between us. Christ tore down the dividing wall, Paul says, making the two into one. The people He died to unite should be the last people on earth quick to assemble for war against their own.

So before you march, send the delegation. Ask what the altar means. It may be a witness, not a wound.

Build witnesses, not divisions.

An old man calls the leaders of a nation together to say goodbye. Joshua, who crossed the Jordan and circled Jericho and divided the land, is now near death, and he gathers the elders and heads and judges and officers of Israel for a final charge. We expect a victory speech. We expect him to celebrate the conquest, to bask in the fulfilled promise, to send them off with encouragement. He does the first part. And then he says something that should make our blood run cold.

**The God Who Kept Every Promise**

Joshua begins exactly where you would expect, with the faithfulness of God. "And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you" (Joshua 23:14). Not one word failed. He has them name it. Every good thing God promised, He delivered. The land, the rest, the inheritance, the victory. They are living proof of a God who keeps His word with absolute reliability.

We love this half of the sermon. A God who keeps His promises is the God we preach and sing about, the faithful One whose word does not return empty. And it is true, gloriously true. Joshua makes them swear to it in their own hearts.

**The Same God Also Keeps His Threats**

But then Joshua turns the truth on its edge, and it cuts. The very same faithfulness that delivered every blessing will deliver every judgment. "But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have come to pass, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land" (Joshua 23:15). The God who is faithful to bless is faithful to judge. If they cling to the remaining nations, intermarry with them, and serve their gods, the same dependable word that gave them the land will take it away.

This is the half of the sermon we want to delete. We have constructed a God whose faithfulness only ever runs in one direction, toward comfort, toward blessing, toward our flourishing. Joshua will not allow it. The reliability of God is not selective. The God who cannot break a promise of grace cannot break a warning of judgment either, because it is the same integrity behind both. To trust His blessings while dismissing His warnings is to believe in a God who is only half real.

I feel the cut of this personally. I quote the promises and skip the threats. I want a God whose faithfulness is all carrot and no edge. But a God who would not really judge sin is a God who would not really keep His word, and a God who would not keep His word could not be trusted to keep the promises I love either. The same faithfulness underwrites both, or it underwrites neither.

**Cling, and Be Careful**

Joshua's command is therefore two-edged. "You shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day" (Joshua 23:8). Cling. Hold fast to the One who kept every word. And be careful, he says, take good care of yourselves, watch your hearts, because the pull of the surrounding nations and their gods is real and the cost of yielding is everything.

This points us, soberly, to Christ. At the cross we see both halves of Joshua's sermon meet in one place. The faithful God did keep every threat against sin, in full, holding back nothing, pouring out the judgment His word required. And He did it on His own Son, so that the same faithfulness that demanded judgment could become the faithfulness that secures our blessing. The edge of God's word fell on Jesus, that the promise might fall on us. But the warning still stands for any who will not cling. The God who judged sin in His Son will not wink at it in those who walk away.

The faithful God also judges.

At the very end, Joshua gathers all the tribes to Shechem, the place where Abraham first built an altar when he entered the land centuries before, and there he makes them choose. Not vaguely, not someday. This day. He stands before a people who have everything, the land, the rest, the fulfilled promise, and he refuses to let them coast into the future on inherited faith. He makes them put their hand to a decision.

**He Rehearses What God Has Done**

Before the demand comes the history. Joshua, speaking for God, walks them back through everything, all the way to the beginning. "Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham... and they served other gods. Then I took your father Abraham" (Joshua 24:2-3). He reminds them that their own ancestors were idolaters, that God reached into a pagan family and took Abraham out of it, that everything they have rests on a God who chose first. He recounts Egypt, the sea, the wilderness, the conquest, every act God performed while they contributed nothing but need.

The choice Joshua sets before them is not a choice between equals. It is a response to a God who has already acted, already chosen, already given. He grounds the demand in grace. Before he says choose, he says remember what was done for you. The summons to decide is built entirely on the foundation of what God did before they could decide anything.

**Put Away the Gods You Are Still Holding**

Then the demand. "Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:14). This is the stunning detail. After all the victories, after the land is taken, they are still holding onto foreign gods. The idols of Mesopotamia and Egypt are still tucked in their tents. The conquest of the land was not the conquest of the heart. They had taken Canaan and still had not let go of the gods they brought with them.

This is the most convicting line in the book for me. I assume that because God has given me so much, my idols must be gone. They are not. I carry the gods of the country I came out of, quietly, into the very rooms where I worship the true God. Possession of the promise did not automatically empty my tent of the idols. Joshua tells them, and me, to put them away, deliberately, by name, today.

**A Choice That Will Cost Them**

"Choose this day whom you will serve... But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). And then, when the people eagerly say they too will serve the LORD, Joshua does something almost no preacher would do. He tells them they cannot. "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God" (Joshua 24:19). He makes the choice harder, not easier. He warns them that this God is holy and jealous and the commitment they are making so cheerfully will cost them more than they imagine. He will not let them choose lightly.

This is the integrity the gospel demands. Joshua refuses to make discipleship sound free of cost. He knows the choice to serve the LORD is the choice to put away every rival, to be exposed, to be held to a holy standard. And the people choose anyway. He sets up a stone as a witness against them, because he knows their hearts, and he is right; the generations that follow will break the covenant they swore that day.

Which is exactly why we need the better Joshua. The first one could make them choose, but he could not make them able. He set a stone of witness against a people he knew would fail. The true Joshua, Jesus, does what the first could not. He not only sets the choice before us; He gives us a new heart to make it, and when we break the covenant, as we surely will, He keeps it for us with His own blood. The stone of witness against us was rolled away from a tomb.

So choose. Put away the gods in your tent. But know that the strength to choose Him comes from the One who chose you first.

Choose the One who chose you.
